stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). State whether \(AB = BA\)? Justify your answer.

_note: PRINTED DEFECT (transcribed as printed, verified at 3x zoom on p-35). A is printed with BOTH sine entries positive, i.e. a symmetric matrix, while B is printed correctly as a rotation matrix with -sin(phi) in the top right. As printed the claim is FALSE: with A=[[c,s],[s,c]] and B=[[C,-S],[S,C]], AB has (1,1) entry cC+sS whereas BA has (1,1) entry cC-sS, so AB != BA unless sin(theta)sin(phi)=0. The intended A is almost certainly [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)],[sin(theta), cos(theta)]], for which AB=BA=rotation by theta+phi. Note the SAME book prints the correct rotation form in Ex 4.6 Q23 and Ex 4.7 Q14, which supports the missing-minus-sign reading.
solution: [Textbook misprint: \(A\) is printed with both sine entries positive, and as printed \(AB \ne BA\), so the statement is false. The intended matrix is the rotation form \(\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\), which this same book prints correctly at Ex 4.6 Q.23 and Ex 4.7 Q.14.]

_derivation: A - (lambda)I = [[1-L, 3],[2, 2-L]]. Singular means determinant zero: (1-L)(2-L) - 3*2 = 2 - 3L + L^2 - 6 = L^2 - 3L - 4 = 0.

stem:
Consider the matrices \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\) out of the given matrix product ...........

i) \((AB)^{T}C\)

ii) \(C^{T}C(AB)^{T}\)

iii) \(C^{T}AB\)

iv) \(A^{T}ABB^{T}C\)
_derivation: Orders: A is 3x3, B is 3x2, C is 3x1. (i) AB is 3x2 so (AB)^T is 2x3; (2x3)(3x1) = 2x1, DEFINED. (ii) C^T C is (1x3)(3x1) = 1x1; then (1x1)(2x3) needs 1 = 2, NOT defined. (iii) C^T A B = (1x3)(3x3)(3x2) = 1x2, DEFINED. (iv) A^T A B B^T C = (3x3)(3x3)(3x2)(2x3)(3x1) = 3x1, DEFINED. Exactly three.

stem: If \(A\) and \(B\) are square matrices of equal order, then which one is correct among the following?
_derivation: Matrix addition is commutative (it is entrywise addition of real numbers), so A + B = B + A always holds. B and C fail whenever B is not the zero matrix; D fails in general since matrix multiplication is not commutative.

stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -2 \\ a & 2 & b \end{bmatrix}\) is a matrix satisfying the equation \(AA^{T} = 9I\), where \(I\) is the identity matrix of order 3, then the ordered pair \((a, b)\) is equal to .......
_derivation: AA^T = 9I means the rows are mutually orthogonal with squared length 9. Rows 1 and 2 already satisfy this (1+4+4 = 9, 4+1+4 = 9, dot product 2+2-4 = 0). For row 3 = (a,2,b): dot with row 1 gives a + 4 + 2b = 0, dot with row 2 gives 2a + 2 - 2b = 0 i.e. a - b = -1. Solving a = b - 1 with a + 2b = -4 gives 3b = -3, b = -1, a = -2. Check the length: 4 + 4 + 1 = 9. So (a,b) = (-2,-1).
|A| = alpha^2 - 4 and |A^3| = |A|^3, so (alpha^2 - 4)^3 = 125, giving alpha^2 - 4 = 5, alpha^2 = 9, alpha = +/-3.
Entrywise subtraction: x - (-3) = 4 gives x = 1, and 6 - y = 4 gives y = 2. All the remaining entries check out (5-1=4, 7-2=5, 1-5=-4, 2-2=0).

_derivation: Equating entries: x = 3; 3x - y = 2 gives 9 - y = 2 so y = 7; zx + z = z(x+1) = 4z = 4 so z = 1; 3y - w = 7 gives 21 - w = 7 so w = 14. This is the first printed alternative.

_derivation: The reversal law for the transpose of a product is (AB)^T = B^T A^T, not A^T B^T; indeed A^T B^T is generally not even conformable. B, C and D are all standard true properties of the transpose.
